sections.overview: The bluethroat is a small, shy, robin-like chat that breeds in damp scrub from Scandinavia across Siberia and winters far to the south. In Britain it is a rare vagrant, seen mostly on migration, with only occasional breeding.
sections.identification: About 13–14 cm long, an adult weighs roughly 17 g and has a wing length near 75 mm. The male’s bright blue throat and chest is bordered by black, white and chestnut bands, with a central spot that is white or chestnut depending on the form. Females are duller, with less blue. The upperparts are brownish grey and the tail has a rusty-red base, with a pale stripe above the eye.
sections.habitat: It breeds in the north in Scandinavia and Siberia, extending across Asia towards the Himalayas, and in scattered parts of central and western Europe and around the Black Sea. It prefers willow thickets on damp ground and stays hidden in dense vegetation.
sections.diet: It feeds mainly on insects and other invertebrates, picked from stems and leaves or from under dead leaves on the ground, and only rarely catches insects in the air. It occasionally takes snails and earthworms, and eats seeds and fruit in winter.
sections.behavior: A shy, secretive bird, it often flicks into the cover of a bush, flashing the chestnut patches at the base of its tail. Western populations winter in the Mediterranean basin and northern Africa, and eastern ones in the Indian subcontinent.
sections.reproduction: The deep cup nest of twigs, grass stems and moss, lined with animal hair, is built by the female and hidden in a grass tuft or shrub; nesting runs from May to July. There are typically one or two broods of five to seven eggs (up to nine). The female incubates for 14–15 days and the chicks fledge after about 14–15 days.
sections.ecology: As a predominantly insect-eating bird of damp thickets, it feeds on invertebrates in the breeding season and switches partly to seeds and fruit in winter. The species shows great variation in the intensity of its blue throat and in the colour and shape of its throat spot.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern. In the UK it is a rare vagrant, with only about 5,000 BTO records, no population estimate and occasional breeding (the latest cited in 2016); it is protected under Schedule 1 and is Amber-listed by the RSPB.
